A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DRE-BO-SSL research. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison, including material moved into v2's appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original optimization experiments on synthetic functions, Tabular Benchmarks, NATS-Bench and multi-digit MNIST, plus appendix ablations.

after.justification: V2 reports original experiments on the same benchmarks, with updated results, expanded ablations and new parameter-learning and runtime analyses.

M1.justification: The optimization loop, label propagation/spreading updates, acquisition maximization and truncated-normal sampling remain unchanged. Entropy minimization for beta already appears in v1 Section 4.1; v2 documents its implementation and use more explicitly without establishing a new method component.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same four synthetic functions, four Tabular Benchmarks datasets, three NATS-Bench datasets and multi-digit MNIST task. Expanded ablations reuse existing functions and scenarios rather than introduce new task or dataset coverage.

E2.justification: Corresponding benchmark comparisons retain GP-EI, GP-UCB and BORE/LFBO using random forests, gradient boosting, XGBoost and MLPs. Sampling analyses retain the same comparator choices. The newly cited MALIBO work is not added as an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: NATS-Bench evaluation extends from 200 to 500 optimization iterations in Figure 6. The pool-sampling study replaces subset sizes 5–1000 with 10–4000 and adds elapsed-time evaluation using a stated 4000-point pool. These substantially revise evaluation budgets and supplementary experimental settings.

E4.justification: V2 adds learned-beta trajectories (Figure 4) and runtime versus subset-size analysis (Figure 13). Unlabeled-point count and distribution studies expand from label spreading on two functions to both classifiers on all four functions. Beta sensitivity and pool-sampling analyses also expand, substantially strengthening examination of parameter dependence and computational cost.

E5.justification: Section 5 changes the reported experiment count from 10 fixed-seed repetitions to 20, with corresponding caption updates throughout. V2 explicitly identifies the reported statistics as sample means and standard errors; v1 shows uncertainty shading without defining it. This is a paper-wide revision of replication and uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Main benchmark and appendix curves are replaced, and v2 adds beta trajectories, runtime measurements and expanded ablation results. Figure 11 newly shows cases where no-transductive learning performs best, such as Branin with label spreading. Updated aggregates and extended NATS-Bench runs should not be interpreted as same-setting performance improvements over v1.

T1.justification: V1 Section 4.3 uses error bounds in Equations 11–13 to support superiority in the proposed setting. V2 Appendix C removes this argument and explains that the cited theory assumes independent, identically distributed data and cannot directly apply to sequential Bayesian optimization. A suitable theoretical analysis is left to future work; the cluster assumption and margin definition remain.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims: identifying classifier overconfidence, proposing DRE-BO-SSL with two unlabeled-data scenarios, and demonstrating empirical effectiveness. The revised supporting analyses do not introduce a new headline contribution.

C2.justification: V2 substantially qualifies the justification for unlabeled data: Appendix C acknowledges the theoretical applicability gap, and Appendices C/F replace v1's clear advantage over no-transductive learning with objective-dependent conclusions. Section 5.2 additionally acknowledges cases where GP methods perform better and softens the MNIST assessment from outperforming baselines to satisfactory performance.

D1.justification: V2 discloses SciPy L-BFGS-B with one initialization for learning beta, per-iteration optimization, 2000-point subsampling for nonsynthetic pool benchmarks, and fixed settings for supplementary studies. It also specifies CPU models and clarifies MNIST image construction. These supplement existing implementation details; both versions still promise code release upon publication.

R1.justification: V2 adds Pan et al. (2023) to connect the exploration/exploitation issue with MALIBO and cites Virtanen et al. for SciPy. It replaces the expected-improvement reference to Mockus et al. (1978) with Jones et al. (1998). The broader positioning relative to BORE, LFBO and semi-supervised learning remains.

P1.justification: V2 makes local prose edits, expands experimental explanations and switches to author-year citations. The analysis moves from Section 4.3 to Appendix C, and limitations move from Section 6 to Appendix H. Despite these reorganizations, the main narrative and most section content remain recognizable.

P2.justification: V2 adds beta-learning and runtime figures, expands several ablation grids, and combines v1 Figures s.1/s.2 into Figure 8. It also extends NATS-Bench axes, revises captions and substantially changes the document template, headings and figure placement. These are substantial display changes beyond numerical updates.

improvement.justification: V2 resolves an important validity problem by withdrawing v1's direct application of non-sequential error bounds and explaining the missing assumptions in Appendix C. Expanded ablations expose limits to the benefit of unlabeled data, while additional repetitions, explicit standard errors and runtime measurements strengthen empirical assessment. Implementation disclosures also improve reproducibility. Although a Bayesian-optimization-specific guarantee remains absent, the paper provides substantially better-supported and more qualified evidence.
